summary:
Bolivia's 2016 Gender Identity Law grants legal recognition of gender identity through an administrative procedure based on self-declared identity. A change of name and legal marker is available without surgery, hormone therapy or a medical diagnosis. Gender identity is a protected ground in the country's anti-discrimination legislation.

The 2009 Constitution prohibits discrimination and protects bodily integrity. Article 15(II) addresses violence and Article 45(V) addresses maternity, while Title VIII of the Penal Code governs abortion.

The 2016 statute was adopted despite low documented voter support for trans rights. Comparative Politics research published in April 2024 found that trans activists obtained access to legislators of the ruling party and that heteronormative provisions were adopted in the same period, because both organised religion and LGBT organisations functioned as constituencies of the governing party.

Partner recognition developed alongside gender-identity recognition. In January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion on gender identity and same-sex partnership, and in December 2020 the Bolivian civil registry began recognising free unions between same-sex couples.

Formal protection has not removed discrimination in practice. The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia recorded the constitutional guarantee against discrimination together with persistent societal discrimination against LGBT people. Bolivia's first virtual LGBTI survey, published in December 2024 by Agencia Presentes, found extensive exclusion of LGBTI people across the country.
tangentialFactors:
The trajectory in Bolivia runs counter to the regional pattern of restrictive legislation. Comparative Politics described the 2016 law as ground-breaking precisely because it advanced at a moment of weak public support, achieved through legislative access rather than broad electoral demand.

Military service offers no clear comparator. A July 2017 Newsweek count identified 18 countries believed to fully legalise LGBT military service after the United States announced a transgender service ban; Bolivia was not singled out in that list, and no source in the inventory confirms the position of openly trans personnel in the Bolivian armed forces.

The 2011 US State Department assessment of Bolivia also addressed arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions and corruption, which bear on how protection is delivered to anyone in state custody.
localsOnly:
Homosexuality remains taboo within the Bolivian armed forces. Reporting by eju.tv and La Razón on 25 August 2014 quoted gay soldiers describing discrimination and sanctions, with testimony given anonymously, while the TLGB collective and human-rights campaigners publicly demanded openness in the military.

Resident same-sex couples have had free unions recognised by the civil registry since December 2020, a change that followed the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of January 2018.

The 2009 Constitution's Article 45(V) frames maternity as a protected status, and abortion is governed by Title VIII of the Penal Code rather than by the gender-identity statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve how the 2016 law is enforced in practice: processing times, fees, regional variation in civil-registry offices, and the number of completed name and marker changes are not sourced here.

No source states whether a changed Bolivian marker is reflected on passports or other documents used at borders, so entry-document consequences for a trans visitor remain unresolved.

Bolivian hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, and any recorded prosecutions under it, are not documented in the sources supplied.

No trans-specific violent incident with a date and outcome appears in the inventory; the evidence for violence risk is limited to documented societal discrimination and the anonymous testimony of gay soldiers.

The position of openly trans personnel in the armed forces, and the sanctions referred to in 2014 reporting, are not specified in the sources.
